stops: Highgate station; Southwood Lane; Park Walk; North Road; Highgate School chapel; Gatehouse

publishedWalks.title: Highgate Village: Tales of History and Mystery — Deborah Greenfield
themes: Advertised 60-minute tour covering residents, architecture, environment, village preservation and folklore; starts at the cemetery entrance and ends at Pond Square. Origin/source family: Highgate Society promotional description, dated 22 August 2025; locator: lines 70–90. ([highgatesociety.com](https://highgatesociety.com/highgate-village-tales-of-history-and-mystery/))
stories: Advertised leads: threatened road widening, Swearing on the Horns, Graham Chapman’s writing, Romantic poets, Dickens settings and ghosts. Nell Gwyn’s window story and claims about poets dying of addiction must not be adopted as established facts from promotional copy. Paid audio was not obtained or heard. ([highgatesociety.com](https://highgatesociety.com/highgate-village-tales-of-history-and-mystery/))

candidates.name: Jacksons Lane arts centre — exterior
candidates.why: A station-area alternative to familiar cemetery stories: investigate community campaigning and a church’s conversion into an arts venue. Intended discovery: residents reshaping local institutions. Present anchor proposed: facade viewed from public pavement, with the actual standing point unresolved. The Open House listing is a discovery lead only; its historical dates have not been accepted as evidence. ([programme.openhouse.org.uk](https://programme.openhouse.org.uk/listings/10874?utm_source=openai))

candidates.name: Pond Square and the village High Street
candidates.why: Explore how the village survived proposed road widening, rather than relying on ghost folklore. Intended discovery: the apparently settled streetscape as a product of civic choices. Proposed anchor: square or High Street pavement. The Highgate Society advertisement supplies the preservation lead, not independently verified episode evidence; locator: lines 72–79, dated 22 August 2025. ([highgatesociety.com](https://highgatesociety.com/highgate-village-tales-of-history-and-mystery/))

candidates.name: Highgate service reservoir — exterior vicinity
candidates.why: A less obvious infrastructure candidate: investigate the relationship between village ponds and piped water. Intended discovery: hidden engineering beneath a village landscape. Proposed anchor: publicly accessible vicinity of the reservoir mound, not entry. Dates conflict: Jones gives 1854, while a London Gardens Trust search lead gives 1846; neither date is selected. ([london-walking-tours.co.uk](https://www.london-walking-tours.co.uk/free-tours/highgate-village-walk.htm))

candidates.name: 3 The Grove — Coleridge-associated exterior
candidates.why: Investigate writing, care and the Gillman household without reducing the poet to an addiction anecdote. Intended discovery: a literary life supported by a household. Proposed anchor: public pavement opposite the private house; no entry or resident-focused commentary. The Coleridge Trust and Friends of Coleridge are fresh specialist leads requiring source reading. ([thecoleridgetrust.com](https://thecoleridgetrust.com/?page_id=178&utm_source=openai))

candidates.name: The Flask — exterior
candidates.why: Investigate the distinction between an old establishment and surviving building fabric, alongside travel and pub customs. Intended discovery: why a prominently displayed date need not date the whole building. Proposed anchor: public pavement, without requiring a purchase. Historic England’s listing is a primary-source lead; building chronology and pub folklore remain unresolved. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1379053?utm_source=openai))

candidates.name: Waterlow Park — higher-ground public viewpoint
candidates.why: Connect a visible London panorama with the conversion of private grounds to public amenity. Intended discovery: landscape and philanthropy rather than simply a scenic pause. Historic England identifies southward views from higher ground; Friends of Waterlow Park describes variable gate times and closure at darkness. Proposed viewpoint and usable gate remain unselected. Locators: listing lines 203–208; Friends page lines 37–40. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1000849))

candidates.name: Lauderdale House and terraced gardens — exterior
candidates.why: Use the house, terraces and steps to investigate successive rebuilding and landscape adaptation. Intended discovery: several historical layers in one visible place. Historic England describes surviving sixteenth-century fabric, later alterations and restoration after fire; locator: lines 209–211. Proposed anchor: park-side exterior terrace, subject to access verification. Nell Gwyn anecdotes are not accepted evidence. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1000849))

candidates.name: Highgate Cemetery — Swain’s Lane entrance exterior
candidates.why: Investigate the cemetery’s architectural threshold and relationship to the hillside without requiring admission. Intended discovery: the burial landscape as part of the neighbourhood, not a celebrity-grave checklist. The published tour explicitly starts outside the western entrance; proposed public-pavement standing point remains unresolved. Interior graves, paid entry and visibility through railings are not promised. ([highgatesociety.com](https://highgatesociety.com/highgate-village-tales-of-history-and-mystery/))

plan.title: Highgate: community, literary households and public landscapes
plan.selectionReason: Provisional selection for brief highgate-beta-v8, schemaVersion 1, using the supplied fresh research and matching 2026-10-06 OSM snapshot. Five supported exterior stops form a coherent progression: residents creating Jacksons Lane, Coleridge within the Gillman household, The Flask's qualified building chronology, Waterlow's gift of grounds, and Lauderdale House's layered fabric. All proposed standing points and station endpoints lie within the supplied offlineMap bounds. Start and finish on the public pavement outside Archway Road exit 3, not at the underground station node; station re-entry through that exit is not promised. Proposed connections are the signal-controlled Archway Road crossing to Jacksons Lane; public street pavements via Jackson's Lane and Southwood Lane toward the village and The Grove; the short connection to The Flask; South Grove and the village pavements to Waterlow Park's mapped northern pedestrian gate; upper park paths to the statue and Lauderdale House; and the open Lauderdale House Gate to Highgate Hill, returning via the village and Southwood Lane to the station exterior. No private hillside paths, house approaches, Bacon's Lane shortcuts or school grounds are intended. Narration remains stationary because the street sections involve hills, junctions and crossing decisions. The 3600-second duration is a target, not a measured result: the router must measure all six legs, and rendered speech, looking time and practical allowance must then be counted with overlap only once. Park inclusion requires posted opening conditions to permit both stops and departure before closure; departure time remains unresolved. Ordinary crossing checks and posted conditions suffice, without field certification. This continuation used one bounded read_map query, no failed retrievals and USD 0 spending; elapsed time and token usage are unavailable. Next action: route this order, verify public-pavement connections and park gate topology, then render and measure original qualified narration. No listening or outdoor visit is claimed.

highgate-beta-v8-survey-c03: omit because reservoir chronology and the proposed ponds-to-piped-water story remain unresolved.

review.summary: Accepted at the combined draft-review stage: no concrete required factual, access, canonical-direction or package defect is established by the supplied evidence. The changes below are advisory and do not veto the tour. This verdict does not certify field conditions, rendered media or a completed playback package.

issues.problem: The story introduces only “Coleridge” and later describes a literary association without plainly identifying him. Listeners with little neighbourhood knowledge may not know why this resident matters.
issues.repair: Owner: writer. Replace “the name to keep in mind is Coleridge” with “the name to keep in mind is the poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge”. Closure evidence: revised first paragraph identifying him without adding an anecdote or extending the story.
issues.evidence: The retained read_page output from the Coleridge Trust introduces “Samuel Taylor Coleridge” and describes Seamus Perry’s talk as concerning “the poet’s life and works in Highgate”. This small addition directly serves the brief’s assumed knowledge.

issues.problem: “That phrase, ‘with their household’” presents the draft’s wording as a quoted phrase, although the source says “he moved with his hosts”. The relationship is accurately conveyed, but the quotation-like framing is unnecessary.
issues.repair: Owner: writer. Change the opening to “That idea—moving with the household—is worth dwelling on.” Closure evidence: revised paragraph preserving the household interpretation without implying a verbatim source quotation.
issues.evidence: The retained Coleridge Trust read_page output states: “He was never to leave the Gillman household. In November 1823, he moved with his hosts to the famous address: 3, The Grove.”

issues.problem: Several consecutive reflections restate public ownership, shared places and layered fabric. The central discoveries are clear, but repeated abstraction may make the final two stops feel less distinct when heard aloud.
issues.repair: Owner: writer. Consider shortening Waterlow paragraph 2 to its first two sentences and removing the final generalisation in Lauderdale paragraph 3. Preserve the gift, surviving southeast range and their qualifications. Closure evidence: revised paragraphs retaining both distinct discoveries and their present anchors; no new research or listening prerequisite.
issues.evidence: Waterlow paragraphs 2–4 repeatedly interpret the same gift as public ownership and shared use. Lauderdale paragraph 3 returns to the layered-building interpretation already developed at The Flask and in its own paragraph 2.
